title: When One Unit Is Too Much
topic: How planned loss, stop distance and unit value determine a risk-based position size, and why the minimum permitted unit may still be too large

scenes.title: ZERO CAN BE THE RIGHT SIZE
scenes.overlay: The minimum unit may still be too large.
scenes.narration: If the smallest tradable unit breaks your risk limit, the disciplined position size may be zero. Size comes last.

scenes.title: SET THE LIMIT BEFORE SIZE
scenes.overlay: Choose the planned loss amount first.
scenes.narration: If the smallest tradable unit breaks your risk limit, the disciplined position size may be zero. Size comes last.

scenes.title: MEASURE THE STOP DISTANCE
scenes.overlay: Stop distance is only one input.
scenes.narration: Measure the distance from entry to the stop. That distance is only one part of the calculation; it is not the loss amount by itself.

scenes.title: CALCULATE LOSS PER UNIT
scenes.overlay: Distance x point or tick value.
scenes.narration: Multiply the stop distance by the instrument's point or tick value to estimate planned loss per unit. Check contract rules and minimum size increments.

scenes.title: CALCULATE, THEN ROUND DOWN
scenes.narration: Divide the planned risk amount by the loss per unit. Round down to the permitted increment. If even one unit exceeds the plan, passing is a valid decision.

scenes.title: PLANNED RISK IS NOT A PROMISE
scenes.overlay: A stop can execute at a different price.
scenes.narration: This is a planning estimate, not a guaranteed loss cap. For a standard stop order, the SEC says the trigger becomes a market order; the execution price can differ. Paper-trading education only; not live-money performance; not investment advice; no guaranteed returns.

instagram_caption:
A risk limit is a ceiling, not a target. Start with the planned loss amount, calculate the loss per unit from stop distance and point or tick value, then size down to the permitted increment. If even one unit is too large, passing can be the disciplined choice. For a standard stop order, the trigger is not a guaranteed execution price.

Sources: CME Group — Proper Position Size: https://www.cmegroup.com/education/courses/trade-and-risk-management/proper-position-size
SEC Investor Bulletin — Stop, Stop-Limit, and Trailing Stop Orders: https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins-15

youtube_description:
If the smallest permitted position size exceeds a pre-defined risk limit, the planned size may be zero. This short explains the relationship between a planned loss amount, stop distance, point or tick value and position size. It also explains why the calculation is a planning estimate, not a guaranteed loss cap, and why a standard stop order can execute at a different price from its trigger.

Sources:

claims.claim: CME Group's position-sizing lesson identifies stop location and the amount a trader is prepared to risk as key inputs to position size.
CME Group illustrates planned risk per contract using stop distance in ticks and the value of each tick.
The SEC states that a standard stop order becomes a market order when triggered; the execution price can differ from the stop price.
